text: Everything in this lesson is something you've already built separately, either earlier in this chapter or back in course nine and course ten. What's new is wiring it into one real architecture: a Deployment running the model server on a GPU node, a Service and Ingress routing traffic to it, an HPA scaling it on a real GPU metric, and the Prometheus and DCGM stack from course ten supplying that metric. This lesson closes the chapter by putting the whole picture together.

Two details matter more here than in a typical web app Deployment. The readiness probe's initialDelaySeconds is set to sixty, not five, because loading model weights into GPU memory genuinely takes real time — a probe tuned for a stateless app's quick startup would mark the pod unready, or kill it, before the model ever finished loading. And pod anti-affinity spreads replicas across different nodes, so one GPU node failure or drain doesn't take out every replica at once.

The Service and Ingress in front of it are exactly the routing pattern from course nine — nothing about them is GPU-specific. A Service gives stable internal routing to whichever replicas are healthy, and an Ingress exposes that Service externally with TLS. The only thing that's changed from a stateless web app is what's sitting behind them: a GPU-backed Deployment instead of a CPU-only one.

The HPA scales on DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL, the real per-GPU utilization metric the DCGM exporter reports to Prometheus and the Prometheus Adapter surfaces as a custom metric — exactly lesson fifteen's pattern, now applied for real. A PodDisruptionBudget with minAvailable: 1 sits alongside it, guaranteeing at least one replica survives a voluntary disruption like a node drain or a cluster upgrade, protecting the availability this whole architecture exists to provide.

Read end to end: a request hits the Ingress, routes through the Service, lands on a warm GPU replica spread across nodes for resilience, while DCGM and Prometheus continuously feed the HPA the signal it needs to add or remove capacity. That's batch versus real-time, serving frameworks, and cost-aware autoscaling, all expressed as one real set of manifests. Chapter five picks up the model lifecycle itself — training, evaluation, deployment, and monitoring for drift.
